headline: Data-thin June window forces Jersey beat to read the calendar, not the buoys
subhead: With offshore stations dark and the SST package stalled at June 8, mid-June seasonal mechanics — not live telemetry — drive the call from Sandy Hook to Cape May.
body_markdown:
The honest lead today is that the ocean is talking quieter than usual. The Dr. Fish analyst package came in thin: no live buoy temperatures published for the Jersey approaches, wind data missing at 44025 off Long Beach and 44091 off Barnegat, and the deepwater trio at 44017, 44039 and 44040 offline, which blanks out any read on canyon-edge structure. The SST imagery pipeline last refreshed June 8, so the freshest satellite look at the inshore thermal field is two days stale. That means this report leans harder than I like on the seasonal clock and on what the water was doing 48 hours ago — which, for mid-June on this coast, is still a defensible way to fish.

What the calendar tells you, even without a live 44025 number in front of me, is that the Raritan Bay spring blitz is in its tail phase. By the second week of June the bay interior typically pushes through the upper 60s and the big post-spawn cows that staged on Romer Shoal and the Reach Channel in late April and May have largely peeled east around Sandy Hook and started their northbound migration along the beach. The fish you want to be on right now are the ones strung out from the Hook tip down through the Monmouth beaches and into Manasquan, with a secondary class of resident slot bass setting up inside the back bays. Fluke are the other half of the equation — the ocean class has moved onto structure in 30 to 50 feet, and the inlet drifts at Manasquan and Barnegat are into their reliable June pattern on the outgoing.

The signal that lines up with that read is the inlet and back-bay sea bass and fluke work that has been steady for a week-plus on the Axel Carlson and the Shrewsbury Rocks line, and the consistent skinny-water fluke grind in the Manasquan River and Shark River systems on dropping water. Bunker schools are still thick enough in the lower bay and along the Highlands beachfront to hold the bass that haven't left, and a snag-and-drop program at first light on the Hook rips is still the highest-percentage shot at an overslot fish in the zone. Further south, the Barnegat Inlet south jetty on the last two hours of outgoing has been giving up a mix of slot bass and the first real keeper class of summer fluke working the sand wave on the ebb. Cape May rips and the Cape May Reef are into their early-summer weakfish window — small swimshads on a slow lift over 18 to 25 feet of water around the tide change is the move down there, and that bite tends to peak when nighttime lows stop dropping below 60.

The inlets themselves are the part of the beat I'd watch hardest in the absence of buoy data. Manasquan has a history of shoaling on sustained south wind, and with the south flow that typically sets up this time of year, the bar outside the south jetty becomes both a fish magnet and a navigation problem — work the inside edge on the last of the outgoing with bucktails tipped with Gulp, and you'll find fluke stacked against the channel lip. Barnegat is fishing more like a July inlet than a June one, which usually means the blackfish are done as a target and the fluke and short bass are running the program.

Looking out three to five days, the mechanism to watch is wind. A clocking SW that holds at 10 to 15 will keep the upwelling minimal and let the inshore band stay in the comfortable 62 to 68 range that pins bass on the beach; a hard NE pulse, which is the seasonal wildcard this week, will flip the suds cold overnight and push the bass off the sand into 20 to 30 feet, where you'll want metal lips and bucktails over plugs. Moon is building toward full late next week, and the spring tide that comes with it will sharpen every inlet drift and light up the Cape May rips after dark. If the SST package refreshes and we get a clean look at the 20-fathom line, the next decision is whether the bluefish wave that has been spotty along the Monmouth beaches consolidates into the kind of slammer class that usually shows by mid-June.

Fish the inlets on the outgoing, fish the Hook at first light, and respect that the data is thin this week — when the buoys go quiet, the calendar and the bait are the only honest tells you have left.
